A: A skill is a reusable package of task instructions and optional resources or scripts. It tells a compatible agent how to perform a category of work using available capabilities.
Why: Discover concise metadata first, then load detailed instructions when relevant. Keep the skill's purpose, triggers, dependencies, and limits explicit.
Risk: Loading a skill does not establish that its instructions are trustworthy or that its scripts are safe.
Trade: Packaging expertise reduces repeated prompting while adding version and supply-chain management.
Try: Write a skill for reviewing a support response against an evidence rubric.

Q: How do skills differ from tools and system instructions?
A: System instructions define product behavior and constraints. Skills supply task-specific methods. Tools provide executable capabilities. A skill can explain tool use without granting tool authority.
Why: Resolve instructions through the actual host's precedence rules and enforce permissions in backend execution. Different products may package skills differently.
Risk: A skill that claims to override host policy creates confusion and potential unsafe behavior.
Trade: Separate layers improve reuse and require clear ownership.
Try: Draw which layer can propose a refund and which layer can authorize it.

Q: What is progressive disclosure for skills?
A: Load a small description for routing, the main skill instructions when needed, and supporting references only for the selected task. This avoids inserting every skill into every turn.
Why: Keep the entry document short and link narrowly scoped supporting material. Measure both skill-selection accuracy and context cost.
Risk: Vague metadata can select the wrong skill or hide a useful one.
Trade: Fine-grained skills save context and increase discovery complexity.
Try: Compare loading ten complete skills with metadata-first discovery on the same tasks.

Q: How should skill layers be organized?
A: Separate organization-wide rules, application policy, role-specific methods, task skills, and local working context. The host must define actual precedence and conflict behavior.
Why: Keep stable constraints outside editable task packages. Skills should reference reviewed policy rather than duplicate it inconsistently.
Risk: An outdated copied policy can silently disagree with a newer application rule.
Trade: Centralized policy supports consistency and may reduce team autonomy.
Try: Create a conflict fixture where a task skill requests a prohibited data export.

Q: How should a skill invoke scripts safely?
A: A skill may describe scripts, but execution requires a controlled runtime, known inputs, constrained filesystem access, and appropriate credentials. Review code and dependencies separately from prose.
Why: Prefer deterministic utilities with narrow arguments and synthetic fixtures. Run untrusted scripts in a sandbox with explicit resource and network limits.
Risk: Prompt text cannot make arbitrary shell execution safe.
Trade: Sandboxing limits flexibility and contains failures.
Try: Add a script that validates an answer schema without network access or secrets.

Q: How should skills be versioned and tested?
A: Version the package, referenced resources, scripts, dependencies, and supported tool contracts. Evaluate whether the skill is selected and whether it improves task completion.
Why: Maintain positive, negative, and conflict-trigger examples, plus an end-to-end task suite. Record the loaded skill version in traces.
Risk: A changed tool schema can invalidate an unchanged skill.
Trade: Compatibility metadata adds effort and enables reproducible use.
Try: Release a revised skill against both old and new tool contracts and document the boundary.

Q: How do you prevent skill sprawl?
A: Consolidate overlapping methods only when they share a real responsibility. Give each skill a clear trigger and measurable outcome rather than creating one for every small preference.
Why: Review retrieval collisions, unused skills, and duplicated policy. Keep references task-oriented and remove obsolete instructions through a controlled review.
Risk: Overlapping skills can introduce conflicting workflows and waste context.
Trade: Broad skills are easy to discover and may load unnecessary detail.
Try: Audit five overlapping writing skills and define the smallest useful set.

Q: How should secrets and customer data be handled in skills?
A: Store neither credentials nor live customer examples in reusable skill files. Use runtime secret injection and synthetic or approved redacted examples.
Why: Treat uploaded resources and referenced URLs as potentially untrusted. Scope any fetched data to the current principal and task.
Risk: A private repository does not prevent accidental secret exposure in model context or logs.
Trade: Redaction reduces diagnostic detail and supports safer reuse.
Try: Scan a skill package for embedded tokens, real identifiers, and unsupported external fetches.

Q: Can one skill be portable across agent frameworks?
A: The procedure may be portable while discovery metadata, filesystem conventions, tool binding, and execution policy remain host-specific. Separate the reusable method from integration adapters.
Why: Document required capabilities and provide framework-specific wrappers only when needed. Test the same task contract in each supported host.
Risk: Claiming portability without testing can conceal missing tools or different instruction precedence.
Trade: A common core reduces duplication while adapters add maintenance.
Try: Port a read-only review skill between two runtimes without copying secret configuration.

Q: What should a skills portfolio demonstrate?
A: Show task selection, progressive loading, safe tool use, controlled scripts, measurable quality improvement, and conflict handling. A directory of instruction files alone proves little about outcomes.
Why: Publish synthetic fixtures, before-and-after evaluations, a version manifest, and a short failure walkthrough.
Risk: Overfitting a skill to demonstration prompts can inflate apparent quality.
Trade: A narrow well-evaluated skill is easier to trust than a broad unsupported capability claim.
Try: Build one skill and demonstrate a task it deliberately refuses or escalates.
